_note: Interview question bank. Edit here, then run: python3 tools/build_interview.py

questions.q: Explain a diffusion model in a few sentences.
questions.a: It is a generative model built from two processes. The forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise to a real image over T steps until nothing but noise is left. A neural network is trained to undo that corruption. To generate, you start from pure noise and apply the network repeatedly, removing a little noise each step, until an image appears.

questions.q: What is the difference between the forward and the reverse process?
questions.a: The forward process is a fixed recipe with no learned parameters: it mixes in noise according to the schedule. The reverse process is what the network learns: given a noisy image and the timestep, it predicts the noise so that one step of cleaning can be taken.

questions.q: What is a noise schedule, and is it learned?
questions.a: It is the list of beta values, one per timestep, saying how much new noise is mixed in at each step. It is chosen before training and never learned. Alpha is 1 minus beta, and alpha-bar is the running product of the alphas. A typical linear schedule uses T = 1000 and beta from 1e-4 to 0.02.

questions.q: Write the one-step shortcut formula and say why it matters.
questions.a: x_t = sqrt(alpha_bar_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) * noise, with noise drawn from a standard Gaussian. It lets training jump to any timestep in one operation instead of adding noise t times, which makes every training step cheap.

questions.q: Why is the shortcut formula valid?
questions.a: Each forward step is x_t = sqrt(alpha_t) * x_(t-1) + sqrt(beta_t) * z. Chaining steps multiplies the signal coefficients (giving sqrt(alpha_bar_t)) and adds independent Gaussian variances, and independent Gaussians add up to another Gaussian whose variance is 1 - alpha_bar_t. So t small steps collapse into one.

questions.q: What does alpha_bar_t tell you, and what are its values at the two ends?
questions.a: It is the fraction of the original signal that survives up to step t. It is close to 1 for small t, and close to 0 at the end (about 4e-5 for the linear schedule above), so the final image is almost pure Gaussian noise.

questions.q: Why must x_T be close to pure Gaussian noise?
questions.a: Sampling starts from a draw of N(0, I). If the schedule leaves residual signal at t = T, the distribution seen in training at the last step differs from the starting point used at sampling time, and quality suffers. This is one motivation for schedules such as cosine, and for zero-terminal-SNR fixes.

questions.q: How does noise prediction relate to score matching?
questions.a: The score is the gradient of the log density of the noisy data. Up to a scale factor it equals the negative predicted noise: score = -epsilon_theta / sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t). Predicting the noise and estimating the score are the same thing in different units, which is why diffusion and score-based models are two views of one idea.

questions.q: What does the network predict, and what is the loss?
questions.a: It predicts the noise that was added to the image. The loss is the mean squared error between the real noise and the predicted noise: loss = mean((real_noise - predicted_noise) ** 2).

questions.q: Walk through one training step.
questions.a: Take a batch of clean images. Draw a random timestep per image and fresh Gaussian noise. Build the noisy images with the shortcut formula. Feed noisy images and timesteps to the U-Net to get predicted noise. Compute the MSE against the real noise, backpropagate, and let the optimizer update the weights.

questions.q: Why use a random timestep per image rather than looping over all timesteps?
questions.a: The full objective is an average over timesteps, so one random timestep per image is an unbiased sample of it. Across many batches the single network sees every noise level, which it needs because sampling visits all of them. Looping over every t for every image would multiply the cost by T for no benefit.

questions.q: Why predict the noise instead of the clean image?
questions.a: The two are interchangeable, since the clean image can be recovered as (x_t - sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) * noise) / sqrt(alpha_bar_t). Noise has unit variance at every timestep, so the loss has a similar scale everywhere, and it worked well in the original DDPM work. Other targets such as v-prediction exist and behave better in some regimes.

questions.q: The loss curve is noisy and plateaus early. Is something wrong?
questions.a: Usually not. Each batch uses random timesteps and random noise, so the loss jitters, and it falls quickly then flattens because the hard part is the fine detail. Judge progress by saving sample images every few epochs, not by the loss number alone.

questions.q: How does the simple DDPM loss differ from the true variational bound?
questions.a: The simple loss drops the per-timestep weighting terms of the bound. That effectively down-weights the easy low-noise steps and emphasizes harder, noisier denoising, which improved sample quality at the cost of a worse likelihood. Improved DDPM adds a learned variance term to recover likelihood.

questions.q: Why a U-Net for the denoiser?
questions.a: The input and output are both images of the same shape. The encoder shrinks the image to capture wide context, the decoder grows it back, and skip connections carry fine detail across so the output can be sharp.

questions.q: What is a residual block?
questions.a: A block whose output is its input plus a learned correction, with a convolution on the shortcut when the channel counts differ. It makes deep networks easier to train because the identity path is always available.

questions.q: What does a skip connection do in a U-Net?
questions.a: It concatenates the encoder feature map at some resolution onto the decoder feature map at the same resolution. The decoder then has access to spatial detail that was lost when downsampling, and gradients get a short path back to early layers.

questions.q: How does the network know which timestep it is looking at?
questions.a: The integer t is turned into a sinusoidal embedding vector, passed through a small MLP, and added into every ResBlock. That tells each block how noisy its input is, so it can behave differently for t = 10 and t = 900.

questions.q: Why a sinusoidal embedding rather than the raw integer t?
questions.a: A bare number gives the network little to work with and no sense that 347 is near 350. Sines and cosines at many frequencies give a rich vector where nearby timesteps look similar. It is the same idea as positional encoding in Transformers, and it is a fixed formula, not learned.

questions.q: Why put self-attention only at the bottleneck?
questions.a: Attention compares every position with every other, so cost grows with the square of the number of positions. At the bottleneck the feature map is smallest, so global attention is cheap there, and it is where long-range relationships matter most.

questions.q: Why does this U-Net use GroupNorm and not BatchNorm?
questions.a: With batch sizes of 4 to 16, batch statistics are noisy, and they differ between training and sampling. GroupNorm normalizes within each sample over groups of channels, so it does not depend on the batch and behaves the same at train and test time.

questions.q: How do you generate an image with a trained model?
questions.a: Start with a tensor of Gaussian noise. For t from T-1 down to 0, feed the current image and t to the U-Net to get predicted noise, then apply the sampling formula to get a slightly cleaner image. The result after the last step is the generated image.

questions.q: Write the DDPM sampling step.
questions.a: x_(t-1) = (1 / sqrt(alpha_t)) * (x_t - ((1 - alpha_t) / sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t)) * predicted_noise) + sqrt(beta_t) * z, where z is fresh Gaussian noise for every step except the last, where it is zero.

questions.q: Why add fresh noise at each sampling step?
questions.a: Each reverse step is a draw from a Gaussian, not a single deterministic point. The injected noise keeps the process stochastic, which gives diversity and stops samples collapsing toward bland, repetitive output. It is left out at the last step so the final image is clean.

questions.q: How does DDIM generate in 50 steps with the same trained model?
questions.a: Each DDIM step estimates the clean image from the current noisy one, then re-noises that estimate to whichever earlier timestep you are jumping to, instead of only stepping from t to t-1. You can therefore visit, say, every 20th timestep. Training is unchanged; only the sampling loop differs.

questions.q: Give the DDIM update with no added noise.
questions.a: First x0_hat = (x_t - sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) * predicted_noise) / sqrt(alpha_bar_t). Then x_prev = sqrt(alpha_bar_prev) * x0_hat + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_prev) * predicted_noise. With no added noise the mapping from starting noise to image is deterministic.

questions.q: Why is the cosine schedule often better than the linear one?
questions.a: Linear destroys the image too early: at t = 500, alpha_bar is about 0.08, so well over half the steps see near-static and teach little. Cosine keeps more signal, with alpha_bar around 0.49 at t = 500, so more training steps land where structure still exists.

questions.q: What else can make generation cheaper?
questions.a: Better solvers that need fewer steps (DPM-Solver style), distillation into a few-step student, and latent diffusion, which runs the whole process in the compressed latent space of an autoencoder so each network evaluation is far cheaper.

questions.q: How do you condition the model on a class label?
questions.a: Embed the label with nn.Embedding and add it to the timestep embedding. Every ResBlock then receives one signal saying both how noisy the input is and which class to produce. No other part of the U-Net has to change.

questions.q: Explain classifier-free guidance.
questions.a: During training, replace the real label with a null label about 10% of the time, so one model learns both conditional and unconditional generation. At sampling run it twice per step and combine: predicted_noise = uncond + scale * (cond - uncond). This exaggerates the direction the label pulls in.

questions.q: What does the guidance scale trade off?
questions.a: Higher values follow the label more strictly but reduce variety and can give harsh, oversaturated images. A value of 1.0 applies no extra push, and around 3.0 is a reasonable starting point for this setup.

questions.q: What does classifier-free guidance cost at sampling time?
questions.a: Two network evaluations per step, so generation is twice as slow. With 50 DDIM steps that is 100 evaluations, still about ten times fewer than the 1000-step unconditional loop.

questions.q: How does text conditioning differ from adding a label embedding?
questions.a: A text prompt is encoded by a separate, much larger text encoder into a sequence of vectors, and the U-Net attends to them with cross-attention layers. A class label is a single index, so adding its embedding to the time embedding is enough.

questions.q: You have 4GB of VRAM. What are your levers?
questions.a: Small resolution (32 or 64), small batch size, mixed precision, a small U-Net (few base channels, 2 to 3 stages), and attention only at the bottleneck. Add gradient accumulation if you want a larger effective batch.

questions.q: What does mixed precision with GradScaler do?
questions.a: Most of the math runs in 16-bit floats, which roughly halves activation memory. Small gradients can underflow in fp16, so the scaler multiplies the loss up before backward and divides the gradients down before the optimizer step.

questions.q: What is EMA and why does it help?
questions.a: An exponential moving average keeps a shadow copy of the weights updated as a slow average of the real ones. Raw weights jitter from batch to batch; the average is smoother and gives visibly better samples. Train with the real weights, generate with the EMA copy.

questions.q: The loss becomes nan. What do you try?
questions.a: Lower the learning rate, add gradient clipping (clip_grad_norm_ with a ceiling of 1.0, after scaler.unscale_ if using mixed precision), and confirm you call scaler.scale(loss).backward() when mixed precision is on.

questions.q: Loss decreases but samples stay pure noise. Where do you look?
questions.a: A falling loss says the model is learning, so first train longer. If the loss looks healthy but sampling still fails, suspect the sampling code: compare the formula line by line, check the timestep indexing, that you sample from the right checkpoint or EMA weights, and that the clamp and rescale to 0-1 match the data normalization.

questions.q: How does gradient accumulation work, and what must you adjust?
questions.a: Run several micro-batches, letting gradients add up, and call the optimizer step once. The effective batch is micro-batch size times accumulation steps. Divide each micro-batch loss by the number of accumulation steps so the summed gradient matches a true large-batch average.

questions.q: Why debug at 32 by 32 before moving to 64 by 64?
questions.a: It is roughly four times cheaper per epoch, and almost every real problem (shape bugs, a bad schedule, a model that never learns) shows up just as clearly at the smaller size. Move up once the pipeline is known to work.

questions.q: What does one forward diffusion step do?
questions.a: It scales the previous image by sqrt(1 - beta_t) and adds Gaussian noise of variance beta_t, so signal shrinks as noise is added while the overall variance stays near 1.

questions.q: Why can you jump straight to step t?
questions.a: Composing Gaussian steps gives another Gaussian: x_t = sqrt(alpha_bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) eps, because independent Gaussians add by summing variances.

questions.q: What is alpha_bar_t?
questions.a: The cumulative product of alpha_s = 1 - beta_s up to t. It is the fraction of the original signal variance that survives at step t.

questions.q: Derive the closed form of the forward process by induction.
questions.a: Assume x_(t-1) = sqrt(ab_(t-1)) x_0 + sqrt(1 - ab_(t-1)) e1. Then x_t = sqrt(alpha_t) x_(t-1) + sqrt(beta_t) e2. The noise terms merge with variance alpha_t (1 - ab_(t-1)) + beta_t = 1 - ab_t, and the signal coefficient is sqrt(alpha_t ab_(t-1)) = sqrt(ab_t).

questions.q: What is the posterior q(x_(t-1) | x_t, x_0) and why is it useful?
questions.a: A Gaussian with mean a weighted average of x_0 and x_t and variance beta_tilde_t = (1 - ab_(t-1)) / (1 - ab_t) beta_t. It is the exact target for each reverse step if x_0 were known, so the model learns to approximate its mean.

questions.q: How does the network's noise prediction give the reverse mean?
questions.a: Replace x_0 by (x_t - sqrt(1 - ab_t) eps) / sqrt(ab_t) in the posterior mean to get mu = (x_t - beta_t / sqrt(1 - ab_t) eps_theta) / sqrt(alpha_t).

questions.q: Why is the simple loss better than the true ELBO weighting for samples?
questions.a: The ELBO weights low-noise steps heavily; dropping the weights emphasises harder, noisier denoising, which improved perceptual quality at the cost of a worse likelihood.

questions.q: What is SNR in diffusion and why do schedules care?
questions.a: alpha_bar / (1 - alpha_bar). A schedule is a path of log-SNR over time; a good one spreads steps over the noise range where structure is formed, which is why cosine beats linear.

questions.q: Compare eps, x0 and v prediction.
questions.a: They are linear reparameterisations of each other given x_t. eps is stable at low noise but amplifies errors at very high noise, x0 is blurry at low noise, and v = sqrt(ab) eps - sqrt(1 - ab) x0 is well scaled at all levels and works with zero terminal SNR.

questions.q: How is a diffusion model related to score matching?
questions.a: The noisy marginal's score equals - eps / sqrt(1 - alpha_bar), so training eps_theta by regression is denoising score matching and eps_theta gives the score up to a known scale.

questions.q: What is the probability flow ODE?
questions.a: A deterministic ODE with the same marginals as the reverse SDE, dx/dt = f(x, t) - 1/2 g(t)^2 score. DDIM and most fast samplers discretise it.

questions.q: What variance should the reverse step use?
questions.a: sigma_t^2 = beta_t or beta_tilde_t are the two fixed extremes. Improved DDPM learns an interpolation between them, which improves likelihood and allows fewer steps.

questions.q: Why must alpha_bar_T be close to zero?
questions.a: Sampling starts from Normal(0, I). If the forward process leaves signal at T the start distribution mismatches the training one, causing artefacts such as washed-out images.

questions.q: Why is diffusion sampling slow?
questions.a: It runs the network once per step for tens to thousands of sequential steps, and guidance doubles the cost.

questions.q: What is the difference between DDPM and DDIM sampling?
questions.a: DDPM adds fresh noise each step (stochastic, 1,000 steps). DDIM with eta = 0 is deterministic and can skip timesteps, giving good images in 20 to 50 steps from the same trained model.

questions.q: Write the DDIM update.
questions.a: x0_hat = (x_t - sqrt(1 - ab_t) eps) / sqrt(ab_t); x_s = sqrt(ab_s) x0_hat + sqrt(1 - ab_s - sigma^2) eps + sigma z, with sigma = 0 for the deterministic version.

questions.q: What is DDIM inversion used for?
questions.a: Because the map from noise to image is deterministic and invertible, running it backwards from a real image finds a noise code that regenerates it, enabling editing by changing the prompt.

questions.q: Why do higher-order solvers need fewer steps?
questions.a: The sampling trajectory is a smooth ODE; second or third order methods such as Heun and DPM-Solver have much lower error per step than Euler.

questions.q: What are ancestral samplers?
questions.a: Samplers that inject fresh noise each step. They never converge to a single image as steps increase, which gives variety but makes results less repeatable.

questions.q: What does classifier-free guidance cost and what are its failure modes?
questions.a: Two network evaluations per step. Large scales oversaturate and reduce diversity; thresholding and guidance rescaling mitigate it.

questions.q: Explain progressive distillation.
questions.a: A student is trained to match two teacher steps with one; the student becomes the next teacher and the number of steps halves each round, down to 4 or 8 steps.

questions.q: What is a consistency model?
questions.a: A function that maps any point on a probability flow ODE trajectory to the same clean sample. It enables one-step generation, trained by distillation or directly with consistency losses.

questions.q: What is flow matching and why does it sample efficiently?
questions.a: Learn a velocity field that transports noise to data along straight interpolation paths. Straight paths are integrated accurately with few ODE steps; rectified flow straightens paths further.

questions.q: How do you compare samplers fairly?
questions.a: At equal number of network evaluations, not steps, with a fixed prompt set and seeds, using distribution metrics and human preference with confidence intervals.

questions.q: How does timestep spacing affect results?
questions.a: Spacing in log-SNR (or the Karras schedule) places more steps where the image changes most; uniform spacing wastes steps at very high noise.

questions.q: Why do diffusion models work in a latent space?
questions.a: Pixel space is large and mostly imperceptible detail. A VAE compresses 8 times per side (about 48 times fewer values), making the denoiser far cheaper and enabling high resolution on ordinary GPUs.

questions.q: What are the main components of Stable Diffusion?
questions.a: A VAE (encoder and decoder), a text encoder (CLIP), a denoiser (U-Net or transformer) with cross-attention to the text, and a scheduler.

questions.q: How does text condition the image?
questions.a: Prompt tokens are encoded to a sequence of vectors; cross-attention layers use image features as queries and text vectors as keys and values, so each position gathers relevant words.

questions.q: What is the VAE scaling factor?
questions.a: A constant (0.18215 for SD 1.x) that normalises latent variance so it matches the unit-variance noise assumption; omitting it gives wrong colours.

questions.q: What does a negative prompt do?
questions.a: It replaces the empty prompt in classifier-free guidance so the sampler is pushed away from the negative description and toward the positive one.

questions.q: Why is the VAE decoder a quality bottleneck?
questions.a: 8x compression loses fine detail such as small faces, text and thin lines; later models use more latent channels and better decoders.

questions.q: U-Net versus diffusion transformer?
questions.a: U-Nets use convolutions and multi-scale structure; DiTs use patch tokens, transformer blocks and adaLN conditioning, scaling more predictably with data and parameters and handling variable sizes naturally.

questions.q: What is MMDiT?
questions.a: A multimodal diffusion transformer with separate weights for text and image tokens that attend to each other in joint attention, used in SD3.

questions.q: Why does attention cost grow so fast with resolution?
questions.a: Self-attention is quadratic in the number of positions; doubling image side quadruples positions and multiplies attention cost by sixteen, hence latents and efficient attention kernels.

questions.q: Describe the inference pipeline step by step.
questions.a: Encode the prompt and an unconditional or negative prompt, sample a seeded latent, run scheduler steps with the denoiser and classifier-free guidance, divide by the scale factor, decode with the VAE, post-process.

questions.q: How would you run Stable Diffusion on 4 GB of VRAM?
questions.a: fp16 weights, attention slicing, VAE tiling, CPU offloading of idle components, memory-efficient attention (xformers or SDPA), smaller resolution, or quantised models.

questions.q: How does SDXL differ from SD 1.5?
questions.a: A larger U-Net (about 2.6B parameters), two text encoders, 1024 px native resolution, size and crop micro-conditioning and an optional refiner stage.

questions.q: What is LoRA and why is it popular?
questions.a: Low-rank adaptation freezes the base weights and trains small matrices B A added to attention layers, using about 0.1 to 1 percent of the parameters, producing tiny files that can be merged or swapped at inference.

questions.q: How many parameters does a rank-r LoRA add to a d_out by d_in matrix?
questions.a: r times (d_in + d_out).

questions.q: DreamBooth versus textual inversion?
questions.a: DreamBooth fine-tunes model weights to bind a rare token to a subject with prior preservation. Textual inversion trains only a new token embedding, so it is lighter but less expressive.

questions.q: What is prior preservation loss?
questions.a: A regularisation that trains on class images generated by the original model so the class word keeps its general meaning and the model does not drift or overfit.

questions.q: How does ControlNet add spatial control without harming the base model?
questions.a: It clones the encoder as a trainable branch fed with the control map and connects it to the frozen U-Net through zero-initialised convolutions, so training starts as an exact no-op.

questions.q: Explain img2img and the strength parameter.
questions.a: Encode the input, add noise only to an intermediate timestep, then denoise. Strength sets how much noise: low keeps the layout, high lets the prompt override.

questions.q: How does inpainting work?
questions.a: Inpainting-trained models receive the mask and masked image as extra channels. Alternatively, at each step replace the known region with a noised copy of the original so only the hole is generated.

questions.q: What failure modes appear when fine-tuning on a few images?
questions.a: Overfitting (the subject appears everywhere, backgrounds copied), language drift, catastrophic forgetting of general abilities; mitigate with fewer steps, lower learning rate, regularisation images and LoRA scale.

questions.q: IP-Adapter versus ControlNet?
questions.a: IP-Adapter injects a reference image's CLIP features through extra cross-attention to transfer appearance or style; ControlNet injects spatial structure maps such as edges, depth or pose.

questions.q: How can you edit a real photo with a text prompt while preserving layout?
questions.a: DDIM-invert the photo to a noise code, reuse or blend cross-attention maps (prompt-to-prompt), regenerate with the edited prompt, or use an instruction-tuned editor such as InstructPix2Pix.

questions.q: How do you choose a LoRA rank?
questions.a: Start at 8 to 32 for styles and 4 to 16 for characters; raise rank for more capacity if underfitting, lower it if overfitting, watching file size and generalisation.

questions.q: Why does generating far from the training resolution cause duplicated subjects?
questions.a: The model learned composition at specific sizes; larger canvases are treated as several images. Use hires fix, tiled approaches, or models trained on multiple aspect ratios.

questions.q: What does FID measure?
questions.a: The Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits of Inception features of real and generated images: lower means the generated distribution is closer to the real one.

questions.q: What does CLIPScore measure?
questions.a: How well an image matches its text prompt, as the cosine similarity of CLIP embeddings.

questions.q: What are the limits of FID?
questions.a: It needs many samples, depends on the ImageNet-trained feature network, ignores prompt alignment, is biased for small sample sizes and can be gamed. Use KID, FD-DINOv2 and human evaluation alongside it.

questions.q: How do you run a human evaluation?
questions.a: Show randomised side-by-side pairs for the same prompt, ask about quality and prompt match, use many prompts and raters, and report win rates with confidence intervals or Elo scores.

questions.q: Why re-caption training images?
questions.a: Web alt-text is short and noisy; detailed synthetic captions improve prompt following and compositional accuracy.

questions.q: What does a data pipeline for image generation involve?
questions.a: Collection, deduplication, quality and aesthetic filtering, safety filtering, re-captioning and bucketing by resolution.

questions.q: How can a diffusion model memorise training images and how do you reduce it?
questions.a: Duplicated images and captions make near-copies likely. Deduplicate, diversify data, limit overfitting, apply output checks and consider differential privacy.

questions.q: What layers of safety do image generators use?
questions.a: Data filtering, model-level safety training, prompt classifiers, output classifiers, provenance watermarking, access controls and red teaming. No single layer is sufficient.

questions.q: How does watermarking help and what are its limits?
questions.a: Invisible watermarks and C2PA credentials signal AI origin, but they can be stripped by edits or metadata removal, so they supplement rather than replace other controls.

questions.q: How would you test for bias?
questions.a: Audit prompt sets across occupations, attributes and cultures, measure demographic distributions of outputs, compare with references, and iterate on data and training rather than only prompt rewriting.

questions.q: What belongs in a good evaluation report?
questions.a: Model, sampler, steps, guidance, seeds, a fixed public prompt set, enough samples, uncurated samples, metrics with intervals, compute-matched comparisons and failure cases.

questions.q: Why compare samplers or models at equal network evaluations?
questions.a: Steps are not equal cost: Heun doubles evaluations and guidance doubles them again, so equal steps can hide large compute differences.

questions.q: How is video generation different from image generation?
questions.a: It adds a time dimension: much more data and the need for temporal consistency. Models add temporal attention or use space-time transformers over compressed video latents.

questions.q: How does diffusion generate audio?
questions.a: Represent audio as a spectrogram or codec latent, diffuse it with a U-Net or transformer, and convert back to a waveform with a vocoder or decoder.

questions.q: What is score distillation sampling?
questions.a: Optimise a 3D representation so renderings from random views are denoised well by a text-conditioned image diffusion model; the diffusion gradient flows through the renderer into 3D parameters.

questions.q: What is the Janus problem in text-to-3D?
questions.a: Multiple faces appear on one object because the 2D prior does not know which view it is seeing; view-dependent prompts and multi-view models reduce it.

questions.q: Why use diffusion for robot policies?
questions.a: It represents multimodal action distributions and generates action chunks conditioned on observations, instead of averaging different valid behaviours.

questions.q: How does diffusion handle discrete data like text?
questions.a: Use a discrete corruption such as masking tokens (absorbing diffusion) or token replacement, or add Gaussian noise to embeddings and round at the end.

questions.q: Why must protein diffusion models be equivariant?
questions.a: A molecule's identity does not change when rotated or translated, so SE(3)-equivariant denoisers build in the symmetry and learn more efficiently.

questions.q: Compare diffusion with GANs, VAEs and autoregressive models.
questions.a: GANs sample in one step but are unstable and cover modes poorly; VAEs are fast but blurry alone; autoregressive models give exact likelihood and scale well but sample sequentially; diffusion is stable and flexible at the cost of multiple steps.

questions.q: What is a spacetime patch?
questions.a: A token covering a small region over a few frames of the compressed video latent; transformers over such tokens handle variable durations, sizes and aspect ratios.

questions.q: Why is long video generation hard?
questions.a: Compute grows with frames, errors accumulate over time, and the model must keep identity, physics and camera motion consistent; solutions include factorised attention, hierarchical generation and autoregressive extension.

questions.q: What is EMA and why do diffusion models use it?
questions.a: An exponential moving average of the weights smooths batch noise; sampling with EMA weights produces visibly better and more stable images.

questions.q: What does gradient clipping do?
questions.a: It caps the global gradient norm so a single bad batch cannot cause a huge step, preventing loss spikes and nan.

questions.q: Why does fp16 training need loss scaling and bf16 does not?
questions.a: fp16 has a small exponent range so tiny gradients underflow to zero; scaling the loss moves them into range. bf16 has fp32's range with lower precision.

questions.q: How would you debug 'loss decreases but samples are noise'?
questions.a: Check sampling code (coefficients, timestep indexing, noise at the last step), use EMA weights, verify data normalisation matches between train and sample, and run a toy overfit test.

questions.q: What is the quickest sanity test for a new diffusion pipeline?
questions.a: Overfit eight images. If the model cannot memorise them, the data, schedule or training loop is broken.

questions.q: What is min-SNR weighting?
questions.a: A loss weighting that caps the weight at high SNR (min(SNR, gamma)), reducing conflicting gradient directions across timesteps and speeding convergence.

questions.q: What is noise offset?
questions.a: Adding a small per-channel constant to the noise so the model learns to change the mean brightness, fixing the difficulty with very dark or very bright images.

questions.q: How does resolution change the best noise schedule?
questions.a: Higher resolution images keep recognisable structure at the same noise level for longer, so the schedule is shifted toward more noise (or the timestep distribution is shifted) at higher resolutions.

questions.q: What parallelism strategies exist for big diffusion models?
questions.a: DDP for data parallelism, FSDP or ZeRO to shard states, tensor and pipeline parallelism for huge transformers, activation checkpointing and gradient accumulation.

questions.q: Why precompute latents and text embeddings?
questions.a: The VAE and text encoders are frozen, so encoding once removes their cost from every epoch and frees GPU memory.

questions.q: Estimate training cost for a 2B parameter denoiser.
questions.a: About 6 x parameters x tokens x images FLOPs; for 2e9 parameters, 1,024 tokens and 1e9 images that is 1.2e22 FLOPs, roughly a thousand A100 GPU-days at realistic utilisation.

questions.q: What is zero terminal SNR?
questions.a: Rescaling the schedule so alpha_bar_T = 0 exactly, typically with v-prediction, so the model trains on the pure noise it will start from at sampling time.

questions.q: Name the components of a Stable Diffusion pipeline.
questions.a: Tokenizer and text encoder, the denoiser (U-Net or transformer), the scheduler, and the VAE decoder (plus an optional safety checker).

questions.q: What does the guidance scale control?
questions.a: How strongly the conditional prediction is exaggerated relative to the unconditional one: higher values follow the prompt more but reduce diversity and can oversaturate.

questions.q: Why does the same seed reproduce an image?
questions.a: The seed fixes the initial noise; with the same prompt, model, scheduler, steps and settings the deterministic pipeline gives the same output.

questions.q: How do you run a large model on an 8 GB GPU?
questions.a: Use fp16 or bf16, efficient attention, VAE tiling, CPU offload of idle components, quantised weights and distilled few-step models.

questions.q: What is a negative prompt and how does it work?
questions.a: It replaces the empty prompt in the unconditional branch of classifier-free guidance, so the sample is pushed away from what it describes.

questions.q: How many sampling steps are typical?
questions.a: 20 to 30 with a good solver such as DPM++ or UniPC; 1 to 8 for distilled models; hundreds for plain DDPM.

questions.q: What is the difference between Euler and Euler ancestral samplers?
questions.a: Ancestral samplers inject fresh noise each step, so results keep changing as steps increase and do not converge to a single image.

questions.q: Why do high resolutions beyond the training size produce duplicated subjects?
questions.a: The model has not seen such compositions and tiles content; generate at native size and upscale or use hires fix.

questions.q: How do img2img strength and inpainting masks work?
questions.a: Img2img adds noise up to a level set by strength then denoises; low strength keeps the layout. Inpainting regenerates masked regions and preserves the rest.

questions.q: How does latency scale with settings?
questions.a: Roughly steps x passes per step x time per denoiser call, plus VAE decode; guidance doubles passes, and attention cost grows with the square of the token count.

questions.q: How would you serve a text-to-image model at scale?
questions.a: Keep models warm in GPU memory, batch requests, queue with priorities, cache embeddings, enforce resolution and time limits, filter outputs and monitor utilisation and latency.

questions.q: How do you make experiments reproducible?
questions.a: Record model and LoRA versions, prompts, seed, scheduler, steps, guidance, size and library versions, and compare several seeds per setting.

questions.q: What is hires fix?
questions.a: Generate at a native low resolution, upsample the latent or image, and refine with img2img at moderate strength to add detail without composition errors.

questions.q: Why combine several LoRAs carefully?
questions.a: Adapters can conflict or amplify each other; weights must be tuned and combinations tested, and strong LoRAs degrade base model quality.

questions.q: What is flow matching?
questions.a: Train a network to predict the velocity along a path from noise to data (for rectified flow x1 - x0 on a straight line) and generate by integrating the ODE.

questions.q: What does a diffusion transformer do differently from a U-Net?
questions.a: It patchifies the latent into tokens and processes them with transformer blocks conditioned on time and text, scaling like language models.

questions.q: What is rectified flow and reflow?
questions.a: Straight-line interpolation between noise and data; reflow retrains on the model's own (noise, sample) pairs to straighten paths so fewer steps suffice.

questions.q: Why do flow models need fewer hyperparameters than DDPM?
questions.a: The loss is plain regression on velocity with no noise schedule or variance parameterisation to tune, though timestep sampling and shifting still matter.

questions.q: What is adaLN-Zero?
questions.a: Adaptive layer norm where the time and condition embedding predicts scale, shift and gate, with gates initialised to zero so blocks start as identity for stable training.

questions.q: Explain MM-DiT.
questions.a: Separate weights for text and image token streams with joint self-attention over the concatenated tokens, allowing two-way information flow.

questions.q: What is timestep shifting?
questions.a: A reparameterisation moving training and sampling toward noisier levels at higher resolutions because neighbouring pixels are more redundant.

questions.q: How do consistency models enable one-step generation?
questions.a: They learn a function mapping any point on an ODE trajectory to the same clean sample, so a single evaluation jumps to the end.

questions.q: Why do real flows still need 20 to 50 steps?
questions.a: The marginal velocity field is curved, and one Euler step uses only the initial velocity, which points at the average of the data and gives a blurry result; more steps or higher-order solvers follow the curve.

questions.q: What is the marginal velocity field and why can a network learn it?
questions.a: The conditional expectation of x1 - x0 given x_t over all consistent pairs. Regression to the per-pair velocity has this field as its minimiser.

questions.q: Compare progressive, consistency, adversarial and distribution-matching distillation.
questions.a: Progressive halves steps repeatedly; consistency enforces trajectory consistency; adversarial distillation adds a discriminator for sharpness; distribution matching aligns the student's distribution with the teacher's through score differences.

questions.q: How does attention cost scale with image size in a DiT?
questions.a: Tokens grow with area, and self-attention cost grows with the square of the token count, so doubling both sides raises attention cost about 16 times.

questions.q: Why use logit-normal timestep sampling?
questions.a: It concentrates training on intermediate noise levels where the model benefits most instead of uniform sampling.

questions.q: How are diffusion models and flow models related?
questions.a: With Gaussian paths the probability-flow ODE of a diffusion model and a flow-matching flow are the same family, differing in time and scale parameterisation and in the training weighting.

questions.q: Why de-duplicate training data?
questions.a: Duplicates cause memorisation and bias the distribution toward repeated content; also decontaminate against evaluation images.

questions.q: What is the first test of a new diffusion implementation?
questions.a: Overfit about ten images until samples reproduce them; failure indicates a bug in the loss, schedule, data range or sampler.

questions.q: How do you find near-duplicate images?
questions.a: Perceptual hashes such as dHash with Hamming distance, or embedding similarity with an approximate nearest-neighbour index.

questions.q: Why re-caption a dataset?
questions.a: Alt text is short and noisy; detailed accurate captions greatly improve prompt following, usually mixed with some original captions.

questions.q: What is caption dropout and why use it?
questions.a: Replacing captions with an empty string about 10% of the time so the model learns an unconditional prediction for classifier-free guidance.

questions.q: What causes washed-out grey samples and how do you fix them?
questions.a: A schedule whose final signal-to-noise ratio is not zero leaks mean brightness; use zero-terminal-SNR rescaling, v-prediction or a noise offset.

questions.q: Samples are oversaturated. What do you change?
questions.a: Lower the guidance scale, use CFG rescaling or dynamic thresholding.

questions.q: How do you detect memorisation?
questions.a: Find nearest training images for generated samples in embedding space and check duplication rates, then reduce duplicates, epochs or model capacity.

questions.q: What is aspect-ratio bucketing?
questions.a: Grouping images of similar shapes into batches so there is no square cropping, and the model learns varied aspect ratios.

questions.q: How can a quality filter harm diversity?
questions.a: A biased scorer rates some styles or groups lower, so strict thresholds shift the mix; compare group proportions before and after and use per-group thresholds.

questions.q: Training loss is low but samples look bad. What do you check?
questions.a: Per-timestep loss (high-noise levels matter), sampler correctness, EMA weights, and direct sample inspection at fixed seeds rather than the averaged loss.

questions.q: How do you fine-tune on a subject without forgetting the base model?
questions.a: Use LoRA with a low learning rate and few steps, a rare identifier token and prior-preservation class images, and caption everything that should vary.

questions.q: What licensing and consent checks belong in a data pipeline?
questions.a: Licence terms and permitted use, opt-out signals, personal data and likeness consent, illegal content removal and provenance records enabling deletion.

questions.q: How do you balance a long-tailed concept distribution?
questions.a: Sample with count raised to a temperature below one, cluster embeddings to balance concepts, up-weight rare high-quality items, and watch for memorisation from repetition.

questions.q: Explain diffusion models to a ten-year-old.
questions.a: Imagine a photo slowly turning into TV static; the computer learns to play the film backwards, so starting from static it can make a new picture.

questions.q: Why predict noise instead of the image?
questions.a: The noise has a simple known distribution at every step, so the target is well-behaved; knowing the noise lets you subtract it to recover the image.

questions.q: What does the seed do?
questions.a: It determines the initial noise and therefore which particular image appears; the prompt determines the kind of image.

questions.q: Explain latent diffusion with an analogy.
questions.a: Work on a small sketch of the poster and enlarge the finished sketch with a decoder, which makes each step far cheaper.

questions.q: Explain classifier-free guidance simply.
questions.a: Compare what the model draws with and without the prompt, and exaggerate that difference to follow the prompt more closely; too much looks burnt and samey.

questions.q: Explain LoRA simply.
questions.a: Small add-on matrices on frozen weights, like sticky notes on a textbook, that nudge the model toward a style or subject.

questions.q: Explain ControlNet simply.
questions.a: A guide such as edges or depth is read by a second network that tells the model where structure must go while the prompt decides what is drawn.

questions.q: Why many small steps?
questions.a: Each step can only correct locally, like walking downhill in fog; smaller steps keep the path accurate, and better solvers or distillation take bigger steps safely.

questions.q: Why are hands and text hard?
questions.a: They are small, highly structured details; with coarse latents, limited examples and weak captions the model approximates them without exact structure.

questions.q: Explain flow matching to an engineer.
questions.a: Pick a path from noise to data, regress a network onto its velocity, then integrate the learned ODE with a few Euler steps; straighter paths need fewer steps.

questions.q: How do you explain the score function to a researcher?
questions.a: The gradient of the log density of noised data; the noise-prediction network estimates it up to a scale, and sampling follows it with added noise (SDE) or without (ODE).

questions.q: How would you explain the privacy risk of diffusion models?
questions.a: They can memorise duplicated training images and regenerate them, so de-duplication, memorisation tests, opt-outs and differential privacy methods reduce the risk.

questions.q: What is the difference between a GAN and a diffusion model, simply?
questions.a: A GAN makes an image in one pass trained against a critic and can be unstable; diffusion makes it over many denoising steps with a stable regression loss and greater diversity, but slower sampling.

questions.q: Why does more guidance reduce diversity?
questions.a: It pushes every sample toward the highest-likelihood region for the prompt, collapsing variation and over-sharpening features.
